title: JWT Security
subtitle: Critical JWT vulnerabilities — the 'none' algorithm attack, weak secrets, missing expiry — and how to implement tokens safely

content.code:
A JWT has three base64url-encoded parts separated by dots:

eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9    ← HEADER
.eyJ1c2VySWQiOiIxMjMiLCJyb2xlIjoidXNlciIsImV4cCI6MTcwMDAwMDAwMH0  ← PAYLOAD
.SflKxwRJSMeKKF2QT4fwpMeJf36POk6yJV_adQssw5c  ← SIGNATURE

Decoded header:  { "alg": "HS256", "typ": "JWT" }
Decoded payload: { "userId": "123", "role": "user", "exp": 1700000000 }

The SIGNATURE is computed by the server:
  HMACSHA256(base64url(header) + '.' + base64url(payload), secret)

The payload is NOT encrypted — anyone can decode it (base64 is encoding, not encryption).
The signature prevents TAMPERING — you can't change the payload without invalidating the signature
(unless the secret is weak, or the server accepts 'none' as the algorithm).

DO store in JWT: userId, role, sessionId, expiry (exp), issued-at (iat)
DO NOT store in JWT: passwords, credit card numbers, PII, secrets
  (the payload is readable by anyone who has the token)

questions.question: A JWT has payload { userId: 123, role: 'admin', exp: 9999999999 } and was signed with alg: 'HS256'. Your JWT_SECRET is 'secret'. What is wrong with this token setup?
options: The expiry (exp) timestamp is too far in the future, but the signature is valid

Both the secret ('secret' is a dictionary word) and the expiry (never expires in practice) are problems — weak secrets can be brute-forced offline, and a token that never expires can be used indefinitely after a breach
HS256 is deprecated and should be RS256
The userId should not be in the JWT payload
questions.explanation: Two independent problems: (1) 'secret' is a terrible JWT secret. JWTs can be brute-forced offline — an attacker who intercepts a token can try dictionary words against the signature without hitting your server. JWT secrets should be a cryptographically random 256-bit value (32 bytes hex). (2) exp: 9999999999 is year 2286 — this token never expires in practice. If it's ever leaked or stolen, it's valid forever. Access tokens should expire in 15-60 minutes. The fact that the payload shows role: 'admin' makes this especially dangerous — a never-expiring admin token stolen from one breach gives permanent access.

faq.q: Should I store JWTs in localStorage or cookies?
faq.a: Cookies (HttpOnly) for the refresh token; memory (React state) for the short-lived access token. Never localStorage for long-lived tokens. localStorage is accessible to any JavaScript on your page — a single XSS vulnerability can steal every stored token. HttpOnly cookies can't be read by JavaScript. Memory is safest but tokens are lost on page refresh, which is why the refresh token (in HttpOnly cookie) is used to re-issue a new access token automatically. This is the recommended pattern.

examples: The 'none' algorithm vulnerability affected many early JWT implementations including php-jwt, pyjwt, and node-jsonwebtoken before they patched it. Applications that relied on these libraries without pinning to a specific algorithm were vulnerable. The lesson: always specify algorithms=['HS256'] (or your chosen algorithm) in both signing and verification calls

In 2022, auth0's jwt-decode library (100M+ downloads/week) had a vulnerability where crafted tokens could bypass expiry validation in some edge cases. Even widely-used, well-maintained libraries have security bugs — stay updated via npm audit and Dependabot
